slides.page_title: Routing Tables and Longest Prefix Match

items: 0.0.0.0/0 matches everything, so it always loses
Fallback by construction, not by priority
No match and no default -> drop + ICMP net unreachable
Advertise 10.0.0.0/8 toward a datacenter
Also route 10.1.2.0/24 out a different link
LPM sends only that /24 the other way
Overlapping plans still route, but assignment collides
10.0.0.0/23 plus 10.0.1.0/24 is a debugging trap

blocks.title: Routes Are Not ACLs
blocks.text: Routes are longest-match, so entry order is irrelevant. ACLs and firewall rules are first-match, top-down. Mixing the two models is a classic error.

items: Scan every entry, keep the longest match: O(N) per packet
~1M BGP routes at line rate makes this unusable
Binary trie: one node per bit, walk destination left to right
Remember the deepest node carrying a route -> O(W), W=32
Patricia trie path-compresses single-child chains
Fewer nodes, less memory — the classic BSD structure
Multibit tries take several bits per level: 8-8-8-8 or 16-8-8
Fewer memory accesses, paid for by prefix expansion
LC- and LPC-tries add level compression for dense regions
Linux uses an LC-trie in fib_trie for IPv4

slides.page_title: Routing Tables and Longest Prefix Match (cont.)

items: Entries stored with don't-care bits, sorted longest-first
Hardware returns the first hit in a single clock cycle
Price: heavy power draw and dollars per entry
RIB = control-plane database of every protocol's routes
FIB = compiled structure the data plane actually reads
Flow-cache lookup was abandoned on backbone gear
Cache-miss floods and DoS destroyed hit rates
Full FIB lookup on every packet is now the norm

blocks.title: What Kills A Router
blocks.text: Prefix count is the real cost driver. Boxes are usually retired because TCAM or FIB size ran out, not because throughput did.

lines: ip route get 8.8.8.8 # entry LPM picked

items: ip route show lists prefix, scope and next-hop
The 'default via ...' line is the 0.0.0.0/0 entry
ipcalc prints network, broadcast, range and host count
Use it to check hand math, never to replace it

rows: pod CIDR caps pods per node

blocks.title: Aggregate Or Be Specific
blocks.text: Aggregating shrinks tables but hides failures. Deaggregating gives precise control but bloats the global table. Pick per link, not per religion.

items: AWS reserves network, router, DNS, future use, broadcast
Each node gets a pod CIDR, often a /24 from a cluster /16
That sizing decision is locked at cluster creation
Firewall and ACL rules are written as prefixes
10.0.0.0/8 in a rule = same bitwise test as a route lookup
Allocate the block you need in 3 years
Renumbering a live network costs far more than reserving
Fixed-length is simpler to automate; VLSM wins when tight
/30 burns 4 for 2; /31 saves 50% over thousands of links
Many small subnets = more routes, gateways, config
NAT hides topology but adds state and blocks inbound
IPv6: 128 bits, no broadcast address, no scarcity
/64 per link by convention
The math becomes hierarchy, not conservation

caption.text: Part 3 of IP SUBNETTING & CIDR. Most people can recite "/24 = 255.255.255.0" and still freeze when handed 172.16.135.9/20 on a live change window. This 10-page handbook rebuilds subnetting from the 32 bits up: masks, magic numbers, VLSM plans, supernetting, the RFC 1918 map, longest prefix match, and how routers actually store a million routes in tries and TCAM. Save it before the next outage picks the exam for you.
